source_file: zhihu_F_1留学生从OPT到H_1B_中间有哪些需要注意的关键节点.txt

heuristics.rule: Start H-1B sponsorship conversations with your employer during OPT year one, not the final year of STEM OPT
heuristics.condition: When you are an F-1 student on OPT with STEM extension eligibility...
heuristics.action: Raise H-1B sponsorship intent with your employer as early as OPT year one
heuristics.because: Most employers require significant internal approval time; waiting until the last year of STEM OPT leaves insufficient runway for employer process and creates unnecessary pressure

heuristics.rule: Track the 90-day unemployment limit as a cumulative total across the entire OPT period, not per job gap
heuristics.condition: When on standard OPT and experiencing any gap between jobs...
heuristics.action: Maintain a running count of total unemployment days across all job gaps during OPT, not just the current gap
heuristics.because: Multiple comments confirm the 90-day cap is cumulative for the entire OPT period; burning 60 days in one gap leaves only 30 days buffer for any future gap

heuristics.rule: Request premium processing for H-1B petition when possible
heuristics.condition: When your employer is filing an H-1B petition...
heuristics.action: Confirm the employer will pay for premium processing ($2,805)
heuristics.because: Premium processing delivers a decision within 15 business days, preventing an extended period of status uncertainty while awaiting adjudication

heuristics.rule: Notify DSO within 10 days of any employer change during OPT
heuristics.condition: When switching employers while on OPT...
heuristics.action: Report the job change to your Designated School Official within 10 days to update SEVIS
heuristics.because: Failure to update SEVIS within the required window creates compliance violations that can jeopardize OPT status

decision_factors.factor: Whether employer is enrolled in E-Verify
decision_factors.why_it_matters: STEM OPT extension eligibility requires the employer to be registered with E-Verify; without this the student cannot qualify for the 24-month extension regardless of their STEM degree
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask HR directly or check the E-Verify employer search tool before accepting an offer if STEM OPT is part of your plan

decision_factors.factor: Whether your degree appears on the official STEM OPT eligible CIP code list
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Not all science or technical degrees qualify; the degree must map to a CIP code on the DHS STEM Designated Degree Program List
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Cross-reference your degree program against the official DHS list before assuming eligibility

decision_factors.factor: Employer's internal H-1B approval process and timeline
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Some employers have multi-layer internal approval requirements that can take months; a short internal runway can cause you to miss the March registration window
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask HR or your manager whether the company has sponsored H-1B before and how long their internal process takes

decision_factors.factor: Cumulative unemployment days consumed during OPT
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Once the 90-day cumulative limit is reached, OPT authorization is violated; this narrows job search flexibility significantly as the limit approaches
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Keep a personal log of exact start and end dates for every employment period; do not rely on memory

decision_factors.factor: H-1B lottery probability given degree level
decision_factors.why_it_matters: US master's degree holders enter the advanced degree pool first, giving them a higher effective probability; this affects how much risk buffer to build into your STEM OPT plan
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Assess whether your degree qualifies for the master's cap (20,000 additional slots); note that historical combined probability across three STEM OPT years is approximately 50-60%

hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The STEM OPT authorization itself stays with the individual, but a new I-983 Training Plan must be submitted for each new employer; many students assume the existing approval carries over without any action
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who job-hop or are laid off and find new roles during their STEM OPT period

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Waiting passively through STEM OPT years without H-1B planning
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: By the final STEM OPT year, the employer's internal approval timeline may be longer than the remaining OPT runway, creating a cliff where the student runs out of status before an H-1B can be filed
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students at employers with slow or bureaucratic HR processes, or at companies that have never sponsored H-1B before

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Using a generic or copy-pasted I-983 Training Plan template
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: USCIS may issue a Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID) for an insufficiently individualized training plan, creating delays and potential gaps in work authorization
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who treat the I-983 as a formality rather than a substantive document requiring job-specific content

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating the 90-day unemployment cap as a per-gap limit rather than a cumulative lifetime limit during OPT
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The rule is counterintuitive; people naturally think of limits as resetting or applying per incident rather than accumulating across the entire authorization period
failure_patterns.consequence: Student unknowingly exhausts their buffer early in OPT, leaving zero tolerance for any future job gap and creating hidden status risk
warning_signs: Student says 'I've been unemployed 60 days so I have 30 days left this time' without considering prior gaps
Student is not tracking a running cumulative total of all unemployment days

failure_patterns.pattern: Submitting a generic, template-based I-983 for STEM OPT
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students underestimate the scrutiny applied to training plans and treat the form as administrative rather than substantive; templates are widely shared in student communities
failure_patterns.consequence: Receipt of a NOID requiring response, potential delay or denial of STEM OPT extension, gap in work authorization
warning_signs: Student copies training plan language from online forums or prior classmates without customizing to their actual job duties
I-983 describes generic skills rather than specific relationship between job tasks and STEM degree field

failure_patterns.pattern: Delaying H-1B sponsorship conversations with employer until the final year of STEM OPT
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students avoid potentially awkward visa conversations, assume employer will raise it, or underestimate how long internal approval processes take
failure_patterns.consequence: Insufficient time for employer internal process before the March registration deadline, missed lottery window, status cliff
warning_signs: Student has never explicitly asked HR about H-1B sponsorship policy
Student is in STEM OPT year two or three without confirmed employer H-1B intent

diagnostic_questions.question: Is your employer enrolled in E-Verify?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether STEM OPT extension is even possible with this employer; without E-Verify enrollment the student cannot get the 24-month extension regardless of degree
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Has the employer previously sponsored H-1B? What is their internal process timeline?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Is the employer willing to enroll in E-Verify, or do you need to consider other employment options to preserve STEM OPT eligibility?

diagnostic_questions.question: How many cumulative unemployment days have you used so far during your OPT period?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: The actual remaining buffer before a status violation occurs; many students underestimate this because they only track the current gap
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If over 60 days cumulative: urgency to secure employment increases significantly; any further gap carries serious risk
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If under 30 days cumulative: relative flexibility remains but should still be tracked precisely

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you explicitly confirmed with your employer that they will sponsor your H-1B, and do you know their internal approval timeline?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether there is a real sponsorship commitment or just an informal assumption; also reveals whether the timeline fits within the remaining OPT window
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: When does their internal process need to start to hit the March registration window?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Begin the conversation immediately; determine if this employer is a viable H-1B path or if you need a contingency plan

diagnostic_questions.question: Does your degree CIP code appear on the official DHS STEM Designated Degree Program List?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student actually qualifies for STEM OPT; students sometimes assume eligibility based on the nature of their work rather than verifying their specific degree classification
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Proceed with STEM OPT planning; confirm DSO has the correct degree information in SEVIS
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Student is limited to 12-month standard OPT; H-1B strategy and timeline must be revised accordingly

industry_realities.common_belief: Changing jobs during STEM OPT means losing your STEM OPT authorization and having to reapply from scratch
industry_realities.actual_reality: STEM OPT authorization is tied to the individual, not the employer; however, the new employer must submit a new I-983 Training Plan, and the employer must be E-Verify enrolled
industry_realities.implication: Students should not avoid legitimate job changes out of fear of losing STEM OPT, but they must ensure the new employer meets E-Verify requirements and complete the I-983 process promptly

industry_realities.common_belief: H-1B registration and STEM OPT are on separate tracks and cannot overlap
industry_realities.actual_reality: You can participate in H-1B registration while actively on STEM OPT; if selected, the H-1B becomes effective October 1st and you transition from STEM OPT to H-1B status at that point
industry_realities.implication: Students on STEM OPT should actively pursue H-1B registration each year rather than waiting until their OPT is nearly expired

industry_realities.common_belief: The H-1B lottery gives everyone roughly equal odds
industry_realities.actual_reality: US master's degree holders enter a separate advanced degree pool of 20,000 additional slots and are drawn first; those not selected in the master's pool then enter the general pool of 65,000, giving them two chances
industry_realities.implication: Students with US master's degrees have a meaningfully higher per-year probability; this should factor into how aggressively they pursue alternative paths vs. waiting for the lottery

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Thinks about the current job gap only; assumes the 90-day limit resets or applies to each individual gap separately
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Maintains a precise running log of all unemployment days since OPT began; treats 90 days as a lifetime budget, not a per-incident allowance
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Naive tracking leads to unknowingly exhausting the buffer early, leaving zero tolerance for future gaps and creating hidden status violation risk

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Avoids bringing up visa sponsorship until forced to by circumstance, assuming the employer will initiate or that there is plenty of time
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Initiates explicit H-1B sponsorship conversation with HR during OPT year one, maps out internal approval timeline, and builds contingency plans before year two
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Late conversations leave insufficient time for employer processes, potentially causing a missed lottery window and a status cliff

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Uses a downloaded template or copies from classmates, filling in minimal customization to satisfy the form requirement
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Writes job-specific content that explicitly connects daily work tasks to the STEM degree field, treating the document as substantive rather than administrative
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Template-based I-983s have triggered NOIDs, causing work authorization gaps for students who treated the form as a formality

community_misconceptions.misconception: The 90-day unemployment limit on OPT resets or applies per job gap, so each individual gap between jobs just needs to stay under 90 days
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Most people intuitively think of limits as applying to discrete incidents; the cumulative nature of the rule is non-obvious and not prominently communicated
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: The 90-day cap is cumulative across the entire OPT authorization period; every day unemployed from the first day of OPT counts toward the same total, regardless of how many separate gaps there are
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: A student who has a 60-day gap early in OPT and assumes they 'reset' then takes another 60-day gap later will have violated their OPT status without realizing it

community_misconceptions.misconception: Changing employers during STEM OPT requires reapplying for STEM OPT from scratch
community_misconceptions.why_believed: STEM OPT involves employer-specific documentation (I-983), which makes it feel like authorization is employer-tied; students conflate the employer requirement with the authorization itself
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: STEM OPT authorization belongs to the individual; a job change requires submitting a new I-983 with the new employer and confirming E-Verify enrollment, but does not require restarting the authorization process
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Students may stay in bad job situations or refuse better opportunities out of unfounded fear of losing their STEM OPT, unnecessarily limiting their career options

real_case_outcomes.situation: Student on STEM OPT submitted an I-983 Training Plan using a widely circulated generic template with minimal customization
real_case_outcomes.decision: Filed STEM OPT extension application with the template-based I-983
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Received a Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID) due to the insufficiently individualized training plan, requiring a response and creating delays in work authorization
real_case_outcomes.lesson: The I-983 must substantively connect the specific job duties to the student's STEM degree; USCIS scrutinizes these documents and generic language is a red flag that triggers adverse action

psychological_barriers.trigger: Student avoids bringing up H-1B sponsorship with employer for months or years, framing it as 'not the right time' or 'I don't want to seem like a burden'
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Fear of rejection or of being seen as a transactional employee; anxiety that raising the visa topic will harm the employment relationship or signal disloyalty
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Student delays the conversation until forced, often until the final STEM OPT year, by which point the employer's internal timeline cannot fit the March registration window
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe the conversation as professional planning rather than a personal ask: 'I want to make sure we're aligned on long-term plans so I can continue contributing here' — and point out that employers who sponsor H-1B need lead time too, so early conversations benefit both sides

psychological_barriers.trigger: Student asks 'what are my options if I don't get H-1B after three tries' in a tone of catastrophizing or paralysis
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Treating H-1B as the only viable path to staying in the US, which amplifies the stakes of each lottery to an existential level
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Decision paralysis, reluctance to build backup plans, over-investment in lottery outcome as identity rather than one variable in a broader career strategy
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Enumerate concrete alternatives (further education resetting OPT, cap-exempt employers, O-1, TN, Canada) as real paths rather than consolation prizes, and encourage building parallel plans from STEM OPT year one rather than sequentially after H-1B failure

reframing_moves.original_framing: How do I make sure I don't lose my STEM OPT if I change jobs?
reframing_moves.reframe: STEM OPT is yours, not your employer's — the question is whether your new employer meets the E-Verify requirement and whether you complete the I-983 correctly
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Shifts the student from a scarcity mindset (protecting something fragile) to an agency mindset (knowing what conditions to verify), which unlocks willingness to pursue better opportunities
reframing_moves.example_language: STEM OPT是绑定到你身上的，但新雇主需要重新提交I-983

reframing_moves.original_framing: I haven't gotten H-1B yet, what should I do now that my STEM OPT is running out?
reframing_moves.reframe: The question is not what to do at the end — it's what parallel paths you should have been building since year one of OPT so you are not in a single-path dependency at this stage
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Moves the student from reactive crisis mode to recognizing a planning failure, which is more constructive and generalizable for future decisions even if the current situation is constrained
reframing_moves.example_language: 从OPT第一年就要和雇主谈H-1B意愿，不要等到STEM OPT最后一年才开始
